snippet.title: Little Debbie The Girl on the Box Is Real and Her Family Built a $2 Billion Empire
snippet.description:
In August 1960, the first cartons of a new snack cake started rolling off a production line at a small bakery in Collegedale, Tennessee, with a full-color illustration of a rosy-cheeked little girl in a straw hat printed across the front of each box. The girl was a real four-year-old child named Debbie, the granddaughter of the bakery's owners, photographed the year before in her favorite straw hat and play clothes. The portrait had been commissioned in secret from an Atlanta pin-up artist and aged up to look about eight or nine, because a real toddler's face was considered too infantile for a national grocery product. When the cartons reached the shipping floor, Debbie's parents learned for the first time that their daughter's face and first name were now the brand identity of every snack cake the family bakery would sell. In the first ten months after launch, the bakery shipped more than 14 million of those cartons across the American Southeast.

In this in-depth episode of Old Money Luxury, we trace how a Depression-era bakery salesman selling five-cent cakes out of the back seat of a 1928 Whippet automobile became the founder of one of the largest privately held food empires in the United States — and how the granddaughter on the box grew up to chair the board of the company that bears her four-year-old face.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

We open on McKee Foods today — a privately held Tennessee company generating approximately $2 billion in annual sales, with more than 6,000 employees across four state factories, over 138 billion individual snacks sold since 1960, and distribution across all 50 states, Canada, Mexico, and Puerto Rico.

We trace the family's ancestral origins in the American South — the Scots-Irish McKees, the Depression-era Chattanooga bakery scene, and the collision of 20th-century mass-production baking with the Seventh-day Adventist industrial community at Collegedale.

We follow O.D. McKee through his early life — the Depression childhood, the Chattanooga bakery routes, and the 1928 Whippet automobile whose back seat carried the first five-cent cakes he sold on commission across the working-class Southeast.

We watch O.D. and Ruth McKee build the first empire — the 1934 marriage, the wholesale bakery experiments, the King Candy Company purchase, the move to the Collegedale bakery in 1957, and the family manufacturing operation that would become McKee Foods.

We reconstruct the first great crisis — the collapse of the King Candy business, the near-bankruptcy years, and the moment Ruth McKee suggested modifying a plain oatmeal cookie into the Oatmeal Creme Pie that would rescue the company and become the flagship product of the entire Little Debbie line.

We walk through the summer of 1960 — Pearl Mann's secret Atlanta commission, the straw-hat portrait aged up to look eight or nine, the packaging design, and the 14 million cartons that shipped in the brand's first ten months on a name and a face O.D. had never cleared with the child's parents.

We follow the second-generation transition — Ellsworth McKee stepping into the executive suite, the mechanization of the bakery lines, the addition of Nutty Buddy, Star Crunch, Swiss Rolls, Zebra Cakes and Christmas Tree Cakes, and the vertical integration that turned a regional Southeast brand into a national grocery staple.

We trace the peak years of the family's private wealth — the four-factory footprint across Tennessee, Virginia, Arkansas, and Ohio, the refusal to sell into every consolidation wave that swept American snack-cake competitors into corporate portfolios, and the Adventist-influenced management culture that kept the company family-held into a fourth generation.

We follow the family through the scandals and tragedies of the peak-power years — the internal disputes, the legal fights, the deaths and losses that unfolded behind the private walls of one of the least publicity-hungry billion-dollar families in America.

We watch the third generation take control — Debbie herself moving from art department to executive suite to board chair, and the family governance structure that has kept an American food empire out of the hands of every private-equity buyer that has come knocking for 65 years.

And we close in the present — 138 billion snacks sold, the bronze sculpture of a four-year-old girl in a straw hat standing in the Tennessee park named after her, and Debbie McKee-Fowler still on the board of the company that put her face on a box in the summer of 1960 without asking her parents' permission first.

snippet.title: The $14 Billion Gas Station That Became a Fast Food Empire: The Sheetz Dynasty
snippet.description:
A nineteen-year-old bought a single dairy store in Altoona, Pennsylvania in 1952 for the equivalent of about $80,000 in today's money — and 74 years later, that store has become a $14 billion convenience empire spanning 800 locations, 26,000 employees, and 107 family shareholders who have refused every buyout offer for three generations. This is the story of how the Sheetz family quietly built one of the largest privately held food businesses in America by pumping gas as a side hustle, betting on touchscreen ordering a decade before anyone else, and engineering a governance structure designed to outlive the founders who built it.

———————————————————

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

———————————————————

Bob Sheetz was a teenager when he bought his brother's struggling dairy store in 1952 — and within two decades, he had pivoted the operation into one of the first food-forward gas stations in America, hiring his younger brother Steve to run the floor while customers learned that the sandwich counter was the real reason to stop.

The breakthrough came in 1973, when Sheetz installed self-service gasoline pumps — a then-radical move that turned the forecourt into a traffic funnel for the kitchen, inverting the convenience-store model decades before competitors caught on.

By the 1990s, the family had locked in the format that still defines the chain today: touchscreen-made-to-order food, 24-hour operations, and a relentless focus on the "MTO" sandwich that has become a cult product across central Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Ohio, Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina.

The family structure is equally engineered — 107 shareholders across three generations, all bound by a governance system that has resisted every private equity overture and kept the company off the public markets despite valuations now estimated at well over $14 billion.

Travis Sheetz, the current CEO and a member of the third generation, has publicly committed to 1,000 stores by 2028 — an aggressive expansion that includes a $1 billion investment in Indiana, a new distribution center in Findlay, Ohio, and the first Sheetz store in the Philadelphia suburbs, opened in February 2026 directly across the street from a Wawa in what insiders are calling the most provocative move in the chain's history.

The rivalry with Wawa — the subject of an Emmy-nominated documentary and described as "the most heated food rivalry in the country" — has defined the eastern Pennsylvania convenience landscape for decades, with both chains tying for second place in the 2025 American Customer Satisfaction Index behind only Kwik Trip.

Sheetz installed its first EV charger in 2012, a full decade before most competitors took the technology seriously, and has since logged over 2 million cumulative charging sessions across 125+ stations in seven states under its own "Rechargery" brand — a bet that mirrors the original 1973 gasoline play.

Steve Sheetz, the brother Bob hired as a teenager and the man who shaped nearly every aspect of the family business, died in January 2026 at age 77 — but the institutional structures he helped design ensure the company will keep running long after the founders are gone.

This is the story of a family that turned a failing dairy store into a $14 billion food empire by understanding, decades before anyone else, that the most profitable square footage at a gas station has always been the kitchen.

snippet.title: Vanderbilt - The $100 Billion Empire That Vanished Documentary
snippet.description:
Dive into the shocking rise and disastrous fall of the Vanderbilt dynasty, the family that built New York City and essentially invented the Gilded Age. At their peak, Cornelius "The Commodore" Vanderbilt and his heirs controlled the railroad and shipping industries, amassed a fortune that would be worth $100 billion today, and built legendary mansions like The Breakers and Biltmore (America's largest private home).

This video exposes the dark secrets, shocking scandals, and ruthless business tactics that underpinned their massive wealth. From Alva Vanderbilt's social climbing and extravagant balls to the eventual collapse of the fortune within three generations, discover how the Vanderbilts lost it all—spending their inheritance on European titles, luxurious yachts, and endless parties.

We analyse the legacy of the "Vanderbilt Curse" and trace the lives of descendants like Gloria Vanderbilt and Anderson Cooper. Learn the financial lessons from the family who went from being the wealthiest in American history to essentially broke.

snippet.title: The "Old Money" Wives Accused Of Murdering Their Husbands And Getting Away With It (Documentary)
snippet.description:
In 1885, a packet of arsenic cost ten cents — and it was the cheapest path to freedom a married woman could find.

In this documentary, we unpack the legal architecture that made poisoning a rational calculation for thousands of Victorian wives: coverture laws that erased women's legal identity at marriage, dower rights that restored everything at widowhood, and a ten-cent powder that bridged the gap between the two. We follow three women — Minnie Wallace, who was acquitted of murder at sixteen and went on to collect three estates from dead men; Florence Maybrick, who was convicted in 38 minutes because she'd committed adultery; and Adelaide Bartlett, who was acquitted of an impossible poisoning and then vanished from history entirely.

You'll learn why a jury deliberated 52 hours to free the most likely killer but needed only half an hour to convict the most likely innocent woman, how a half-million signatures couldn't undo a broken system, and why the real defendant in every case was never the woman in the dock — it was the law itself.

If you're interested in true crime, legal history, or the hidden economics of marriage and power, this is the story behind the story: the system that manufactured its own criminals. Watch, then tell us in the comments — was the system that produced these cases ever truly innocent?

snippet.title: The Marshall Field Dynasty: Death, a Brothel and the Cover-Up That Owned Chicago
snippet.description:
On a November evening in 1905, the founder's only son was shot inside his 43-room mansion on Prairie Avenue, and the family announced he had been cleaning his gun. Almost no one in Chicago believed it. Almost no one in Chicago dared say so in print. The whispers told of a famous brothel, a body carried home in the dark, and a deathbed confession that ran in newspapers across the country and in not one Chicago paper. The same fortune that had built the cathedral of commerce on State Street had bought something far less visible: the ability to decide what Chicago's newspapers would print.

In this in-depth episode of Old Money Luxury, we trace the Marshall Field dynasty across five generations — from a farm boy in Pumpkin Hollow, Massachusetts, to the State Street store that drew 200,000 shoppers a day, to the press empire that could rewrite a death, and finally to a will so carefully drawn it became its own form of damage on the descendants it was meant to protect.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

We open in the dressing room at 1919 South Prairie Avenue on November 22, 1905 — the official story of an accidental gun cleaning, the four days Marshall Field Jr. lay dying at Mercy Hospital, and the version Chicago's papers all agreed to print.

We follow the founder out of Pumpkin Hollow, Massachusetts — the farm boy who walked into Deacon Davis's general store in Pittsfield, learned never to give credit, and arrived in Chicago in 1856 with the conviction that the future of retail belonged to the man who treated his customers like ladies.

We trace the rise of Field, Leiter & Company into Marshall Field & Co. — the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, the 1872 fire that destroyed the rebuilt store, and the Marble Palace on State Street that became the largest department store in the world.

We step inside the Field philosophy — "Give the lady what she wants," the no-questions return policy, the bridal registry, the personal shopper, the Walnut Room, the elevators, the bargain basement, and the engineering of the modern American department store one innovation at a time.

We meet Nannie Scott Field — the founder's wife who fled to Nice in the 1880s and lived in self-imposed European exile until her death in 1896, leaving behind a Prairie Avenue mansion full of rooms her husband no longer entered.

We follow Marshall Field Jr. — the only son, the heir, the husband, the father of three, and the man whose adult life Chicago's society pages described as one long pleasant blur until the night the gun went off.

We walk down South Dearborn Street to the Everleigh Club — Minna and Ada Everleigh's $250,000 brothel with its perfumed fountains, gold piano, and the rumour that would not die: that Marshall Field Jr. had been shot there, by a woman named Vera Scott or by his own hand, and carried back to Prairie Avenue before the police could arrive.

We reconstruct the cover-up — the Tribune, the Daily News, the Inter Ocean, the Herald, all reporting the official line in lockstep, and the single confession that ran in newspapers from New York to San Francisco and in not one Chicago paper.

We follow the founder himself — Marshall Field Sr., who outlived his son by eleven weeks, died of pneumonia at the Holland House in New York in January 1906, and left an estate of $118 million structured into a trust designed to last fifty years.

We trace the will's long shadow — Marshall Field III's nervous breakdowns and his founding of the Chicago Sun, Marshall Field IV's magna cum laude Harvard career and institutionalization, Marshall Field V selling the Sun-Times to Rupert Murdoch in 1983, and the careful protection that became its own form of damage across three successive generations.

And we close on what's left — the clock still hanging over the State Street entrance, the Walnut Room still serving chicken pot pie, Marshall Field's rebranded as Macy's in 2006, and the dressing room at 1919 South Prairie Avenue, now somebody's living room, where the truth about the evening of November 22, 1905, is the one piece of information the most powerful family in Chicago succeeded in burying so completely that not even history has been able to recover it.

snippet.title: The Family Behind America's Most OBSESSIVE Cult Brand (You've Never Heard of Them): Wawa
snippet.description:
There is a convenience store chain so beloved that people tattoo its logo on their bodies, hold weddings inside its locations, and defend its honor in op-eds. Its hoagie has been declared the official sandwich of Philadelphia. Kate Winslet called it mythical. A Florida governor offered to name a town after it. The company is Wawa, generating an estimated $18.64 billion in annual revenue across 1,100+ stores. The Wood family has owned it across five generations and 223 years — and almost no one outside the Mid-Atlantic has ever heard of them.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

The story begins in 1803, when a member of the Wood family lit the furnace of an iron foundry in Millville, New Jersey. Formally incorporated in 1865 as Millville Manufacturing Company, the operation ran on iron and later textiles, and the capital it produced funded what came next.

In 1890, George Wood relocated to Delaware County, Pennsylvania, purchased 1,000 acres in a township already called Wawa, and imported Guernsey cows from the British Crown dependency for their high-fat milk. The town's name came from an Ojibwe word for snow goose, popularized by Longfellow's 1855 poem "The Song of Hiawatha."

In 1902, with raw milk genuinely sickening children across Pennsylvania, Wood arranged for doctors to certify his milk sanitary and trademarked the slogan "Buy Health by the Bottle." The Wawa goose appeared on dairy packaging from the early 1900s onward.

What dismantled the dairy fortune was not a competitor or a market crash but the household refrigerator. By the early 1960s, the milkmen were redundant. Grahame Wood — George's grandson, shaped by service in World War Two and Korea — saw it happening, traveled to Ohio to study a friend's convenience store model, and opened the first Wawa Food Market on April 16, 1964 at 1212 MacDade Boulevard in Folsom, Pennsylvania.

By the end of the 1960s, Wawa had grown to nearly 80 locations. The hoagie arrived in 1975, sold organically by store managers because customers wanted it. The Shorti Hoagie launched in 1992. Hoagiefest followed in 2008. Self-serve touchscreen ordering kiosks were installed in every store in 2002 — more than a decade before McDonald's.

In July 2003, two Wall Street investment banks arrived at Wawa's headquarters to begin formal IPO planning. CEO Dick Wood killed it on the spot. "I felt like a skunk at a picnic." To buy out the Fidelity-managed trust stake for $141 million and the McNeil family's Tylenol-fortune block, he turned to the employees themselves. Seventy percent opted in and over-subscribed the ESOP offering, raising $59 million internally.

Shares valued at $900 each in 2003 were worth $14,000 by 2020 — a 1,455% increase over seventeen years. Inc. magazine reported that many Wawa employees have retired as millionaires. By 2025, the ESOP exceeds $2 billion and accounts for more than 40% of the company.

In 2015, Wawa changed the rules: departing employees were now required to sell their shares immediately upon separation, at $6,940 to $7,652 per share. Within five years, the same shares were worth $14,000. Two class action lawsuits — Pfeifer v. Wawa and Cunningham v. Wawa — settled for $25 million and $21.6 million respectively. Wawa admitted no wrongdoing.

The Florida expansion began on July 18, 2012, when the first store opened in Orlando across from SeaWorld. Within five weeks, five locations. By the mid-2020s, Florida had more Wawas than Pennsylvania. Governor Rick Scott reportedly offered to name a Florida town after the company.

Jeremy Plauche tattooed the logo on his inner bicep because his Louisiana friends refused to believe the place existed. Johnny Knoxville got one during a Jackass shoot in West Chester. Scott Gaddis and Cindy Richardson got married inside the Wawa in Abingdon, Maryland in 2008. Tina Fey referenced the Wawa parking lot on SNL because in Philadelphia the parking lot is itself a cultural venue.

On December 10, 2019, Wawa detected malware on its payment processing servers that had been harvesting credit and debit data since March. The final scope reached approximately 34 million compromised cards. Settlements totaled approximately $48.5 million.

Forty-seven thousand associates currently work at Wawa, more than 40% of them holding shares. The Wood family — nearly 200 descendants of George Wood — owns the majority through trust structures engineered to keep the enterprise private for up to 150 more years. The goal is 1,800 stores by 2030. They have given almost no interviews. No Wood has appeared on a magazine cover. They have no apparent plans to introduce themselves.

In eighteen ninety five, Alva Vanderbilt walked away from her marriage with a settlement worth ten million dollars, a Newport mansion built from five hundred thousand cubic feet of marble, and custody of her three children. It was the most spectacular divorce in American history. But what nobody reported was this: before she could hire a lawyer, before she could file a single document, Alva Vanderbilt needed to solve a problem that every unhappy wife in America shared. Under the law that governed her marriage, she did not legally exist. Every dollar she touched belonged to her husband. Every contract she signed was void. She was, in the precise language of the courts, civilly dead. And a dead woman cannot sue for divorce. So how did she do it? How did any of them do it?

snippet.title: The Tragic Murder Mystery of The U-Haul Family Inheritance (Documentary)
snippet.description:
This in-depth, full-length documentary tells the story of L.S. Shoen, the Navy veteran who built U-Haul from a single welded trailer in a 1945 Oregon milk house into a national fleet of more than 100,000 vehicles, lost control of the company to his own sons in a 1986 boardroom coup, watched his daughter-in-law Eva Berg Shoen shot dead in a Telluride mountain house in August 1990, won a $1.47 billion jury verdict in Phoenix in 1994, and died on a Nevada highway in 1999 in a single-vehicle crash the family has disputed ever since.

---------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

---------------------

Leonard Samuel Shoen was born on a leap day in 1916 in McGrath, Minnesota, financed his way through Oregon State by running four beauty parlors at once during the Depression, and started welding orange-and-white trailers in his in-laws' dairy barn in the summer of 1945.

By the end of 1959, 42,600 U-Haul trailers were on American roads, and L.S. Shoen — father of twelve children from two marriages — had built one of the most recognizable consumer brands in the United States from a $5,000 stake.

On November 8, 1986, his eldest sons Edward "Joe" Shoen and Mark Shoen executed a boardroom coup that stripped their father of operational control of the company he had founded.

On August 6, 1990, L.S.'s daughter-in-law Eva Berg Shoen, the Norwegian-born wife of his son Sam Shoen, was shot dead in the family's Telluride mountain home, in a crime the local handyman Frank Marquis later confessed to in 1993.

In 1994, a Phoenix jury returned a $1.47 billion verdict in a family lawsuit, then one of the largest in American history, that exposed the full scale of the inheritance war the trailer fortune had created.

On October 4, 1999, L.S. Shoen died on US-95 in Nevada in a single-vehicle accident that the Clark County coroner ruled in a way significant members of his family have disputed for more than two decades.

snippet.title: The Morton Family: From Controlling America's Salt Industry To Disappearing Overnight
snippet.description:
In 1999, the Philadelphia chemical giant Rohm & Haas acquired Morton International for $4.9 billion in cash and stock — a 43 percent premium over the pre-announcement share price — and the Morton family name was legally separated from the industrial enterprise that had carried it for more than a century. The blue canister remained. The umbrella girl remained. The slogan remained. The family did not. At its peak, the company that Joy Morton had built from a $10,000 investment in a Chicago salt agency in 1880 controlled at least a third of America's entire salt supply — a dominance so comprehensive that the Supreme Court's 1948 ruling against the company in FTC v. Morton Salt became a foundational precedent in American antitrust law, still cited in scholarship today. The Morton Salt Girl, first introduced in 1914, was ranked number 9 on AdAge's authoritative list of the Top 10 Advertising Slogans of the 20th Century. And the family that created her traces its American roots to a French Huguenot minister who survived the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572, and its industrial empire to a patriarch who was expelled from the University of Michigan twice, lost four consecutive gubernatorial elections, founded Arbor Day, served as United States Secretary of Agriculture, and died editing a libertarian newspaper funded by his sons.

———————————————————

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

———————————————————

Julius Sterling Morton was born in 1832 in Adams, Jefferson County, New York, the eldest of three children — and was expelled from the University of Michigan twice before his 1854 graduation date for "general remissness and inattention to all his college duties," eventually receiving his degree only in 1858 after the controversy had cooled.

He married Caroline Joy French in October 1854, and on the very day of their wedding the newlyweds departed for the Nebraska Territory — purchasing 160 acres of windswept prairie outside Nebraska City in 1855 for $200, and building a modest four-room frame house that they would remodel seven times into the eventual 52-room Arbor Lodge mansion.

Over fifty years, the Mortons introduced more than 270 varieties of trees and shrubs to the property, including at least ten specimens that would qualify as Nebraska state-champion trees — and on January 4, 1872, J. Sterling Morton stood before the Nebraska State Board of Agriculture and proposed the resolution that created Arbor Day.

Nebraska held its first Arbor Day on April 10, 1872, with estimates placing the total number of trees planted that day at over one million — and today it is observed in all fifty states and in multiple countries worldwide.

Morton ran four times for the Nebraska governorship between 1866 and 1892 and lost every time — a Civil War-era Democrat who had opposed Lincoln, his political ambitions were permanently capped by the Union patriotism of frontier Nebraska — but in 1893 President Grover Cleveland appointed him Secretary of Agriculture, a position he held until 1897.

His eldest son Joy Morton, born in 1855, entered the salt business in 1880 by investing $10,000 in the Chicago salt agency E.I. Wheeler & Co. — and within five years had taken over and renamed it Joy Morton & Company, beginning the consolidation that would build one of the most powerful commodity monopolies in American history.

By the early 20th century, Morton Salt produced upwards of 600,000 tons of evaporated salt annually plus an additional 400,000 tons of rock salt — controlling at least a third of America's entire salt supply, and operating at the center of an industry that federal regulators repeatedly found was organized around systematic price-fixing and market allocation.

In 1914, a Good Housekeeping advertisement introduced the Morton Salt Girl — the umbrella, the blue canister, the rain, the freely flowing salt — and the slogan "When it rains it pours," which AdAge later ranked number nine on its definitive list of the Top 10 Advertising Slogans of the 20th Century.

Joy Morton founded the Morton Arboretum in Lisle, Illinois, in 1922 — endowing it with 735 acres and laying the groundwork for what is now one of the most significant arboreta in the world.

In 1948, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled against Morton Salt in FTC v. Morton Salt Co. — a foundational antitrust decision establishing that discriminatory pricing could be presumed harmful without proof of actual competitive injury, still cited in antitrust scholarship today.

snippet.title: Every Grocery Giant Tried to Buy This Family's Stores. They Said No Every Single Time: Wegmans
snippet.description:
For a hundred and ten years, every major grocery conglomerate ever assembled has tried to buy the same family's stores — and the family's answer, across four generations, has been the same: no, thank you. Wegmans Food Markets operates 114 stores across ten states, generates an estimated $12.5 billion in annual sales, employs over 53,000 people, has appeared on Fortune's Best Companies to Work For list for 29 consecutive years, and has never sold a single share of equity to anyone outside the family. Customers tattoo the logo on their bodies. Cher declared her love on Twitter. High school students staged a musical about the store.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

In 1915, a young man named John Wegman began selling fresh produce to Rochester housewives door-to-door from a pushcart. His brother Walter joined him, and on January 30, 1916, the brothers formalized the enterprise as the Rochester Fruit and Vegetable Company.

In 1930, while America was reeling from the Great Depression, the Wegmans opened a 20,000-square-foot store with a cafeteria large enough to seat 300 people — an almost unimaginably large retail food space at a time when grocery shopping meant a clerk fetching items from behind a counter. The flagship introduced refrigerated display windows, vaporized water sprays on produce, in-store seating, and one-stop shopping — concepts that would define the modern American supermarket.

In 1950, Walter's son Robert Wegman became president. His first decision was to raise employee salaries — decades before "employee experience" became a corporate concept. Under his leadership, Wegmans pioneered self-service formats, was the third retail chain in America to adopt electronic cash registers, launched private-label products in 1979, and turned grocery stores into destinations with in-store cafés, bakeries, and childcare areas.

By the time Robert stepped down as chairman in 2005, he had grown the company from five stores to seventy across five states with $3.8 billion in annual revenue. He passed away in April 2006 at 87.

The graveyard of regional grocery chains that said yes to acquirers is long. A&P liquidated in 2015. Winn-Dixie went bankrupt. Lucky Stores, Jewel-Osco, Acme, and Star Markets were all absorbed into the Albertsons-Kroger consolidation wave. Whole Foods sold to Amazon in 2017 for $13.6 billion — and within 18 months Harvard Business School researchers documented a devastating culture clash.

The Wegman family watched every stage of it. In 2015, they repurchased every outstanding share from store managers — removing even the theoretical pathway by which outside pressure could ever force a sale. The family now owns above 90% of voting equity through Wegman Enterprises.

The Wegmans Employee Scholarship Program, launched in 1984, has awarded over $150 million to more than 48,000 employees with no obligation to return after graduation. The company opens only two to three new stores per year — not because it cannot fund faster expansion but because the cultural socialization process cannot be accelerated.

Colleen Wegman has served as President and CEO since 2017. Her sister Nicole leads the Wegmans Brand. When Danny Wegman appointed Colleen, he stated the family's north star plainly: "The time has come to create a structure for the future that will allow us to remain strong, vibrant and family-owned." Not competitive. Not profitable. Family-owned.

snippet.title: The Marine Who Took a Mexican Recipe and Built a $15 Billion Empire: The Wild Story of Taco Bell
snippet.description:
In 1948, a twenty-five-year-old Marine veteran named Glen Bell opened a hot dog stand on Mount Vernon Avenue in San Bernardino, California, and noticed a Mexican restaurant across the street with a line wrapping around the building every night. The restaurant was Mitla Cafe. The recipe was a hard-shell taco invented by a Jalisco immigrant named Lucia Rodriguez. Glen Bell ate there for years.

-------------------------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------------------------

Glen William Bell Jr. was born in Lynwood, California in 1923. His Depression childhood was spent riding freight trains and selling blackberry pies door to door under the name "Mrs. Dye's Homemade Pies."

He enlisted in the United States Marine Corps in 1943 and was assigned as a cook in the Pacific theater. The Marine Corps galley taught him portioning, cleanliness, speed, and the operational discipline that no civilian culinary education could have produced.

In 1948, at twenty-five, he opened Bell's Drive-In on Route 66 in San Bernardino. A few miles away, the McDonald brothers had already cornered the burger market. Bell needed a different idea. The idea was staring at him from across the street.

Mitla Cafe had opened in 1937. Lucia Rodriguez had developed a hard-shell taco — tacos dorados — adapted from the Lenten potato-stuffed tacos of her Jalisco childhood, refilled with ground beef, cheddar, lettuce, and tomato. Customers, including César Chávez, lined up nightly.

Bell ate at Mitla for years, befriended the family, and persuaded their head chef Gloria Hoyle to teach him the technique. He fashioned his own fry basket and added tacos to his hamburger menu. His first taco customer said: "That was good, gimme another."

It took Bell fourteen years to land on the formula. He opened Taco Tia in 1954 selling hard-shell tacos for nineteen cents. He opened El Taco with different partners. He sold his interest, took the proceeds, and resolved to build something entirely under his own control.

On July 6, 1962, the first Taco Bell opened at 7112 Firestone Boulevard in Downey — a 400-square-foot mission-style building roughly the size of a two-car garage. The original menu: tacos, burritos, tostadas, Chiliburgers, and frijoles, all priced at nineteen cents.

The first Taco Bell was funded by forty shares at one hundred dollars each, held mostly by Bell's family. The first franchise opened in Torrance in 1964. The hundredth location opened in Anaheim in 1967.

On February 13, 1978, PepsiCo acquired Taco Bell for approximately $125 million in stock. Bell was fifty-five. He had built the entire company without venture capital and without compromising his vision. PepsiCo had been so unable to compete with Taco Bell that it had been running its own failed taco concept called "Taco Kid" through Pizza Hut.

In 1997, PepsiCo spun the restaurants out as Tricon Global, which rebranded as Yum Brands. The Doritos Locos Taco launched in March 2012 and sold one hundred million units in ten weeks. Within eighteen months, the product crossed one billion dollars in sales. CEO Greg Creed called it definitively the biggest launch in Taco Bell history.

The chain that made Mexican food America's most popular fast-food category could not sell that food in Mexico. Two attempted launches, in 1992 and 2007, both failed. As one local observer summarized: "It's like Mexicans coming up and trying to sell us hot dogs." The second attempt rebranded the chain as "American food" and renamed the taco itself the "tacostada." Every Mexican location closed by 2010.

Glen Bell died of Parkinson's in 2010 at eighty-six. His ashes were scattered off the coast of Torrance near his first franchises. The plaque at the Mt. Soledad National Veterans Memorial reads: "The skills obtained in the Marine Corps launched Corporal Bell's career as the Founder of Taco Bell."

Lucia Rodriguez died in 1981. Her grandson Michael Montaño and his cousin Steve Oquendo still run Mitla Cafe today, on the same Mount Vernon Avenue corner where Glen Bell first watched the line.

snippet.title: The Gilded Age Opera House That Redefined Who Ran New York
snippet.description:
In 1883, the oldest families in New York held just 18 opera boxes, and they refused to sell a single one to the richest man in the country. So the new money built its own opera house, the Metropolitan, and turned a private insult into an open war over who really ran the city. What followed pulled in the Vanderbilts, J.P. Morgan and Jay Gould, crowned Mrs. Astor in her jeweled box, survived a fire that gutted the building, and ended with the wrecking ball in 1967. This is the forgotten story of the Gilded Age, when a fight over a few velvet seats decided the shape of American society.

Former Massachusetts Congressman Barney Frank, known for championing LGBTQ+ rights and financial regulation during his three decades in the House of Representatives, has died at the age of 86.

Long before his congressional tenure, Frank traveled to Mississippi in 1964 to volunteer for the Freedom Summer project. As a teenager in New Jersey, Frank had been deeply affected by the murder of Emmett Till and "couldn't justify not going" after witnessing the deep roots of racism in American society.

He spoke to American Experience on the 50th anniversary of Freedom Summer.
